With \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), both are \(2 \times 2\), so \(AB\) is defined and is \(2 \times 2\). Each entry is (row of \(A\))\(\cdot\)(column of \(B\)).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2(1)+4(-2) & 2(3)+4(5) \\ 3(1)+2(-2) & 3(3)+2(5) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2-8 & 6+20 \\ 3-4 & 9+10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 26 \\ -1 & 19 \end{bmatrix}\).

With \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), the product \(BA\) is \(2 \times 2\).
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1(2)+3(3) & 1(4)+3(2) \\ -2(2)+5(3) & -2(4)+5(2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+9 & 4+6 \\ -4+15 & -8+10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 10 \\ 11 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Note that \(BA \neq AB\), so matrix multiplication is not commutative.

The product of two \(2 \times 2\) matrices is \(2 \times 2\).
\(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -b & a \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a(a)+b(b) & a(-b)+b(a) \\ -b(a)+a(b) & -b(-b)+a(a) \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} a^{2}+b^{2} & -ab+ab \\ -ab+ab & b^{2}+a^{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a^{2}+b^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & a^{2}+b^{2} \end{bmatrix}\).

Here the first matrix is \(3 \times 1\) and the second is \(1 \times 3\); the product is \(3 \times 3\). Each entry is (element of the column)\(\times\)(element of the row).
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1(2) & 1(3) & 1(4) \\ 2(2) & 2(3) & 2(4) \\ 3(2) & 3(3) & 3(4) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 6 & 9 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\).

A \(2 \times 2\) times a \(2 \times 3\) gives a \(2 \times 3\) matrix.
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1(1)+(-2)(2) & 1(2)+(-2)(3) & 1(3)+(-2)(1) \\ 2(1)+3(2) & 2(2)+3(3) & 2(3)+3(1) \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} 1-4 & 2-6 & 3-2 \\ 2+6 & 4+9 & 6+3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & -4 & 1 \\ 8 & 13 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).

We must show \(F(x)\,F(y) = F(x+y)\), where \(F(x) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos x & -\sin x & 0 \\ \sin x & \cos x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Compute the product:
\(F(x)\,F(y) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos x & -\sin x & 0 \\ \sin x & \cos x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \cos y & -\sin y & 0 \\ \sin y & \cos y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Entry \((1,1)\): \(\cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y = \cos(x+y)\).
Entry \((1,2)\): \(-\cos x \sin y - \sin x \cos y = -(\sin x \cos y + \cos x \sin y) = -\sin(x+y)\).
Entry \((2,1)\): \(\sin x \cos y + \cos x \sin y = \sin(x+y)\).
Entry \((2,2)\): \(-\sin x \sin y + \cos x \cos y = \cos(x+y)\).
The third row and third column give \(0,0,1\). Hence
\(F(x)\,F(y) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(x+y) & -\sin(x+y) & 0 \\ \sin(x+y) & \cos(x+y) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = F(x+y)\), as required.

Let \(P = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(Q = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(PQ = \begin{bmatrix} 5(2)+(-1)(3) & 5(1)+(-1)(4) \\ 6(2)+7(3) & 6(1)+7(4) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 1 \\ 33 & 34 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(QP = \begin{bmatrix} 2(5)+1(6) & 2(-1)+1(7) \\ 3(5)+4(6) & 3(-1)+4(7) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 5 \\ 39 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \(\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 1 \\ 33 & 34 \end{bmatrix} \neq \begin{bmatrix} 16 & 5 \\ 39 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\), we have \(PQ \neq QP\).

Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), first compute \(A^{2}\):
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3(3)+(-2)(4) & 3(-2)+(-2)(-2) \\ 4(3)+(-2)(4) & 4(-2)+(-2)(-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\).
Also \(kA - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 3k & -2k \\ 4k & -2k \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3k-2 & -2k \\ 4k & -2k-2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Setting \(A^{2} = kA - 2I\) and comparing corresponding entries:
\(3k-2 = 1 \Rightarrow k = 1\); \(-2k = -2 \Rightarrow k = 1\); \(4k = 4 \Rightarrow k = 1\); \(-2k-2 = -4 \Rightarrow k = 1\).
All entries give the same value, so \(k = 1\).

Write \(t = \tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\), so \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -t \\ t & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(I + A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -t \\ t & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad I - A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Using the half-angle identities \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\) and \(\sin\alpha = \dfrac{2t}{1+t^{2}}\), compute the right-hand side:
\((I-A)\begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha + t\sin\alpha & -\sin\alpha + t\cos\alpha \\ -t\cos\alpha + \sin\alpha & t\sin\alpha + \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\).
Evaluate each entry:
\(\cos\alpha + t\sin\alpha = \dfrac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}} + \dfrac{2t^{2}}{1+t^{2}} = \dfrac{1+t^{2}}{1+t^{2}} = 1\).
\(-\sin\alpha + t\cos\alpha = \dfrac{-2t}{1+t^{2}} + \dfrac{t(1-t^{2})}{1+t^{2}} = \dfrac{-t-t^{3}}{1+t^{2}} = -t\).
\(\sin\alpha - t\cos\alpha = \dfrac{2t}{1+t^{2}} - \dfrac{t(1-t^{2})}{1+t^{2}} = \dfrac{t+t^{3}}{1+t^{2}} = t\).
\(t\sin\alpha + \cos\alpha = 1\) (same as the first entry).
Therefore the right-hand side equals \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -t \\ t & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I + A\), which proves the identity.

Let the amount invested in the first bond (5%) be \(x\), so the amount in the second bond (7%) is \(30000 - x\). Writing the annual interest as a matrix product of the investment row with the interest-rate column:
\(\begin{bmatrix} x & 30000-x \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{5}{100} \\ \frac{7}{100} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1800 \end{bmatrix}\).
This gives \(\dfrac{5x}{100} + \dfrac{7(30000-x)}{100} = 1800\), i.e. \(5x + 210000 - 7x = 180000\), so \(-2x = -30000\) and \(x = 15000\).
Hence \(\textrm{Rs }15000\) is invested in the first bond and \(30000 - 15000 = \textrm{Rs }15000\) in the second bond.

Let \(x\) be invested in the first bond (5%) and \(30000 - x\) in the second bond (7%). Using matrix multiplication for the total interest:
\(\begin{bmatrix} x & 30000-x \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \frac{5}{100} \\ \frac{7}{100} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2000 \end{bmatrix}\).
Thus \(\dfrac{5x}{100} + \dfrac{7(30000-x)}{100} = 2000\), i.e. \(5x + 210000 - 7x = 200000\), so \(-2x = -10000\) and \(x = 5000\).
Hence \(\textrm{Rs }5000\) is invested in the first bond and \(30000 - 5000 = \textrm{Rs }25000\) in the second bond.

Convert dozens to units: \(10\) dozen chemistry \(= 120\), \(8\) dozen physics \(= 96\), \(10\) dozen economics \(= 120\) books. Arrange the quantities as a row matrix and the selling prices (Rs 80, 60, 40) as a column matrix. The total amount is their product:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 120 & 96 & 120 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 80 \\ 60 \\ 40 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 120(80) + 96(60) + 120(40) \end{bmatrix}\).
\(= \begin{bmatrix} 9600 + 5760 + 4800 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 20160 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence the bookshop will receive \(\textrm{Rs }20160\) from selling all the books.

Multiply left to right. First, the \(1 \times 3\) row times the \(3 \times 3\) matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1+4+1 & 2+0+0 & 0+2+2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
Now multiply by the column \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ x \end{bmatrix}\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ x \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6(0) + 2(2) + 4(x) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 4x \end{bmatrix}\).
Setting this equal to the zero matrix \(O\): \(4 + 4x = 0\), so \(x = -1\).

Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), compute \(A^{2}\):
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3(3)+1(-1) & 3(1)+1(2) \\ -1(3)+2(-1) & -1(1)+2(2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
Also \(5A = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(7I = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\).
Then \(A^{2} - 5A + 7I = \begin{bmatrix} 8-15+7 & 5-5+0 \\ -5+5+0 & 3-10+7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = 0\), as required.

Multiply the row by the \(3 \times 3\) matrix first:
\(\begin{bmatrix} x & -5 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x-2 & -10 & 2x-8 \end{bmatrix}\),
since column 1 gives \(x(1)+(-5)(0)+(-1)(2)=x-2\), column 2 gives \(x(0)+(-5)(2)+(-1)(0)=-10\), and column 3 gives \(x(2)+(-5)(1)+(-1)(3)=2x-8\).
Now multiply by the column \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} x-2 & -10 & 2x-8 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = (x-2)x + (-10)(4) + (2x-8)(1)\)
\(= x^{2} - 2x - 40 + 2x - 8 = x^{2} - 48\).
Setting \(x^{2} - 48 = 0\) gives \(x^{2} = 48\), so \(x = \pm 4\sqrt{3}\).

Arrange the annual sales as a \(2 \times 3\) matrix (rows = markets, columns = products \(x, y, z\)) and the unit sale prices as a \(3 \times 1\) column. The total revenue in each market is the product:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 10000 & 2000 & 18000 \\ 6000 & 20000 & 8000 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2.50 \\ 1.50 \\ 1.00 \end{bmatrix}\).
Market I: \(10000(2.50) + 2000(1.50) + 18000(1.00) = 25000 + 3000 + 18000 = 46000\).
Market II: \(6000(2.50) + 20000(1.50) + 8000(1.00) = 15000 + 30000 + 8000 = 53000\).
So the total revenue is \(\begin{bmatrix} 46000 \\ 53000 \end{bmatrix}\): \(\textrm{Rs }46000\) in market I and \(\textrm{Rs }53000\) in market II.

The unit costs are Rs 2.00, Rs 1.00 and 50 paise \(=\) Rs 0.50 for \(x, y, z\). The total cost in each market is:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 10000 & 2000 & 18000 \\ 6000 & 20000 & 8000 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2.00 \\ 1.00 \\ 0.50 \end{bmatrix}\).
Market I cost: \(10000(2) + 2000(1) + 18000(0.5) = 20000 + 2000 + 9000 = 31000\).
Market II cost: \(6000(2) + 20000(1) + 8000(0.5) = 12000 + 20000 + 4000 = 36000\).
Using the revenues from part (a) (Rs 46000 and Rs 53000), the gross profit \(=\) revenue \(-\) cost:
Market I: \(46000 - 31000 = \textrm{Rs }15000\).
Market II: \(53000 - 36000 = \textrm{Rs }17000\).
Hence the gross profit is \(\textrm{Rs }15000\) in market I and \(\textrm{Rs }17000\) in market II.

The known matrix is \(2 \times 3\) and the result is \(2 \times 3\), so \(X\) must be \(2 \times 2\). Let \(X = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(X\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a+4b & 2a+5b & 3a+6b \\ c+4d & 2c+5d & 3c+6d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & -8 & -9 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\).
From the first row: \(a+4b = -7\) and \(2a+5b = -8\). Solving, multiply the first by 2: \(2a+8b=-14\); subtracting gives \(-3b = 6\), so \(b = -2\) and \(a = -7 - 4(-2) = 1\). (Check: \(3a+6b = 3-12 = -9\).)
From the second row: \(c+4d = 2\) and \(2c+5d = 4\). Multiply the first by 2: \(2c+8d=4\); subtracting gives \(3d = 0\), so \(d = 0\) and \(c = 2\). (Check: \(3c+6d = 6\).)
Hence \(X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
